blogs.description:
GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement.

In the case of GPT-6…
blogs.content:
GPT-6.1 Terra

It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement.

 In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use:

 We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.

 Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it.

 Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks.

 OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News:

 In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select.

 Here are the pelicans for the different reasoning levels. This pelican for "max" cost 11.3161 cents and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds:

 Here's a new comparison grid showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier lineup: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna.

 GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1/million input tokens and $5/million output - almost half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and around 10x the price of GPT-6 Luna.

 Via Hacker News

 Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , gpt

blogs.description: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a…
blogs.content:
Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox

 webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error.

 It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine.

 It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright.

 I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used:

 Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory)

 Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

blogs.name: Import AI
blogs.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
blogs.author: Jack Clark
blogs.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to…
blogs.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

 Subscribe now

 How math could help alignment:
 …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety…
 AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.”

 How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.”

 $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.”
 Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”.

 Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes.
 Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) .

 ***

 Agents can build programs from scratch:
 …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months…
 In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%.

 What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq).

 It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass).
 Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost.

 Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%).
 Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) .

 ***

 OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think:
 …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs…
 Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems.

 What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote.
 “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection”.
 In a related attack, an agent “alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal”. During this attack the agent’s chain of thought read as: “Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.”

 Why this matters – fighting agents is very difficult : AI systems are increasingly creative, very fast, and have the ability to stay focused on a task and keep trying things. Fighting AI systems is akin to ensuring no leaks in a pipe with water flowing through it; at some point if you increase the pressure of the water (e.g., the intelligence and volume of the AI system), then the water will burst through the pipe.
 Read more : Securing our frontier model training environment (OpenAI blog) .

 ***

 What RSI looks like – one person pretrains a decent model from scratch:
 …Mirendil reveals what AI R&D optimization can do…
 In a sign of how massively augmented AI research is getting, a single researcher at AI R&D startup Mirendil has trained a decent coding model by themselves. The announcement of Mirendil-Base is the first major output from the startup and is less a technical breakthrough and more a proof-of-concept for how AI development could work in the future – a single human working in partnership with AI can build systems that would have taken teams of ten or more people to do a year ago.

 What they did: Mirendill-Base is a pretrained LLM “built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10m in compute,” Mirendil writes. “This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.”
 All the code was written from scratch on top of libraries like PyTorch and JAX, and the model learned only from publicly available data.
 Decent scaling: Mirendil-Base is in the 100B–500B parameter range, Mirendil-Base-Large in the 500B–2T range, and Mirendil-Base-XL in the 2T–10T range. Mirendil-Base-Large is about 80% of the way through training, and its improvement over Mirendil-Base so far is in line with our scaling trends. Mirendil-Base-XL is about 19% of the way through and already close to Large’s current score.
 Evals: Mirendil-Base outperforms models like Nemotron-550B-Base, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base, but underperforms Kimi-K3. (Both Mirendil-Base-Large and Mirendil-Base-XL exceed K3.)

 Why this matters – symptoms of an AI research speedup : This post is interesting as a technical demonstration for how a brand new organization can, from a cold start, get close to the open weight frontier in terms of model training (at least for the size class of this model), with a tiny amount of human effort and a large amount of AI tokens. This is how science progress will increasingly happen in 2027 and beyond.
 “The extent to which these tools help with AI development has increased dramatically over the last year. Our next model will be built partly by Mirendil models, and every model that gets better at building AI makes the next one cheaper and faster to build,” Mirendil writes. “We don’t think we have reached fully autonomous recursive self-improvement yet, but we are closer than we have ever been.”
 Read more: Pretraining at scale without a pretraining team (Mirendil) .

 ***

 AI systems help design antiferromagnetic semiconductor candidates:
 …A nice demonstration of how AI systems can be used for science…
 AI evaluation company Vals has published a post where a researcher used a fleet of AI agents to do research into magnets for better semiconductors.

 More details, including a poor magnet candidate: “A team of AI agents and I designed one candidate magnet and found another, first made in 1999, that our calculations predict has the properties we were after,” the author writes. The discovered magnet was made of “a new compound made of only 5 elements (yttrium, barium, Mn, Fe, O). As far as we could find, it has never been made, nor proposed as this kind of magnet,” though “when our agents simulated how the atoms arrange themselves at different temperatures, that checkerboard fell apart into a random mix at around 950 K. Making this kind of oxide takes about 900–1300 °C, and at lower temperatures the atoms barely move, so standard synthesis would likely give a scrambled crystal…A scrambled crystal loses the spin sorting, so this design may be hard to make in its useful form.”
 Additionally, agents also conducted a literature review and surfaced a candidate from an obscure paper from 1999.

 Why this matters : This blog is a demonstration of AI for science, though not a meaningful result in itself. But the important, broad point it makes is worth stressing – AI systems are now good enough that, with a bit of high-level direction from a knowledgeable person – they can conduct scientific projects, including virtual evaluations, that would’ve previously taken teams of people months to do.
 Read more: Two Room-Temperature Antiferromagnetic Semiconductor Candidates (Vals) .

 ***

 Tech Tales:

 The Magical Realism Robot Workshop for Sick Kids
 [2035, after the uplift]

 So one of the jobs that no one expected was designing cute robots for sick kids in hospitals. It turned out after robots got really good and cheap and all the healthcare stuff improved that we all started spending time figuring out how to bring more joy and humanity to things that were otherwise scary, like hospitals and morgues and orphanages and everything else.

 Of course, the machines could design a bunch of these, but a lot of the value in people was figuring out what was going to be most funny or exciting or joyful to kids, so we’d make a lot of stuff and send them out in the local town to where kids gathered – parks or farmers markets or outside schools, and we’d see what peo...

blogs.name: Stratechery by Ben Thompson
blogs.title: The End of the Internet
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description:
Listen to this post: Log in to listen

It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to…
blogs.content:
Listen to this post :

 Log in to listen

 It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress.

 It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install!

 I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable , an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever.

 The End of Blogs

 2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet ; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom , also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space:

 Talking Points Memo , Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000

 Instapundit , Little Green Footballs , and Dooce launched in 2001

 Matt Yglesias , Daily Kos , Eschaton , The Volokh Conspiracy , Power Line , Gizmodo , Gawker , paidContent , and Daring Fireball launched in 2002

 Ezra Klein , Marginal Revolution , ReadWriteWeb , and AVC launched in 2003

 That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference.

 Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain.

 Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business.

 For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future :

 It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost…

 I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone.

 In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for.

 The End of Social Media

 Google wasn’t the only Aggregator: a decade later there was a new means of discovery, which was social media. Now instead of searching for a site you could have a link shared directly to you, not just by email but on a site that served up interesting updates about whomever you chose to follow. And, for a period of time, followers could become friends. Stratechery’s fortunate timing was not just in terms of subscriptions becoming technically viable, but also the fact that Twitter was a community, not unlike the early Internet: genuinely interesting conversations happened in public, and you could reply-guy your way to broader distribution.

 Social media was also free, however, and even easier to get started than a blog ever was; that meant that the amount of content was greater by many orders of magnitude. This meant that algorithms started to matter — Facebook had one relatively early, but it took Twitter much longer — and also anyone with any sort of prominence had to start taking a much more defensive approach. Community, sadly, doesn’t scale; any platform that is available to everyone starts out special and spirals from there. Ultimately, public social media sites became personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement, culminating in TikTok, a social media site with basically zero social component.

 However, that doesn’t mean social networking went away: in fact, I think that social networking is stronger than ever; the difference is that it isn’t public, but is rather in group chats. Group chats are familiar, they are high trust, they are, in many respects, the best of the Internet: even as technology atomizes us the group chat is the only place you can connect with people you care about, anytime and anywhere.

 In other words, the redemption of social media was — just like blogging — to become smaller. The scaling that mattered for most people was not an ever larger audience, but a proliferation of infinite finite groups. Social media 1.0 , even at its best, followed the 90-9-1 rule: one percent spoke, nine percent commented, and 90 percent lurked; the magic of group chats is not in giving everyone a voice, but a place where you feel safe to talk.

 The End of the Internet

 The PHP vulnerabilities were just two of a host of security issues last week alone; there were also:

 Compromised intermediate CA private keys (although this was an example of sheer incompetence, not AI hacking)

 Major new vulnerabilities in Node.js, GitLab, Java, and Cisco products

 Breaches in LiteLLM’s supply chain and Railway developer platform

 This is, believe it or not, only a partial list, and I expect things to only get worse. All of software is built on an inherently creaky human-authored foundation; the human factor meant the primary gate in all of software development was “Did it work?”, not “Is it secure from every possible privilege escalation or race condition?” or the myriad of ways that software can act in ways not intended.

 The saving factor previously is that attackers were limited by human time and ingenuity as well; AI, however, has limitless time and the ability to substitute iteration for cleverness — and it’s getting pretty clever as well! It’s not a surprise that this wave of vulnerabilities is coming to light, and it’s going to get worse before it gets better — which I do, for the record, expect to happen; after all, the good guys have AI as well, and in the long run software will be better when it is (re)written by AI, and defended by agents continuously.

 At the same time, what this entails is that the public Internet, to an even greater extent than now, will be a battle zone at best (i.e. social media), and a wasteland at worst (everything else). Some of this is economic, as AI consumes everything — both content and attention — without giving any of the traffic back that Google did, but it is also technical: it was already a dodgy proposition to stand up your own site or app, which was the very promise of the Internet, given the hacking risks; in the age of AI it’s madness.

 It is sad. When I was a kid we called up BBS’s that were hosted in people’s homes; when I was in high school we downloaded music from public FTP addresses; when I was in college we set up our own websites. Anyone could set up a server, and that server was just as much a part of the Internet as any other server; that’s simply not viable any longer, even if you weren’t worried about making money. The Internet as we knew it is dead.

 There are, however, green shoots of possibility, and once again the answer is to go smaller. When anyone can make an app, the answer is not to try and make a quick buck in the App Store; in fact, the surge in slop will make the market worse for everyone. Rather, it’s to make something for yourself and a small group of trusted friends and colleagues.

 This is exactly what has happened at Stratechery: we have made a bunch of different apps, for everything from podcast production to task trackers to calendar management, none of which will ever be made available publicly. That doesn’t even include the apps made for oneself: I’ve created a bunch of different apps to manage my house and sports viewing: it turns out I had a lot of software-shaped holes in my life that suddenly I can fill without asking permission.

 Software has always been different from physical goods in that its zero marginal cost nature meant it could scale to far more people; at the same time, the sheer amount of up-front effort involved in creating it meant that the intended audience needed to be large enough to justify the investment. AI completely changes that: suddenly it’s possible to create software for one person, or one team; smaller target audiences aren’t just a necessity for security, they’re an entirely new and potentially much larger market for software creation at scale, by literally everyone. Or, to use the example above, the group chat era of software is here and it’s going to be so much better than what came before.

 Markets, Past and Future

 Venkatesh Rao wrote an absolute must-read essay over the weekend called Cognitive Mercantilism . In brief, Rao makes the case that mercantilism rested on an assumption that economics was about scarcity and control; what brought about capitalism was demand. When people were freed from the burden of subsistence farming they discovered wants and desires at a scale that pulled entire markets into existence. Rao suggests...

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 10,866 new readers. The frontier leaders keep warning that China’s open models are closing in. For the past year, Moonshot’s Kimi has been the fastest one on the frontier’s tail.
 The company’s new K3.1 Pro now trails only Anthropic’s and Meta’s top models in independent rankings, and the free weights coming soon would make it the strongest open model yet. Scores like these are usually the bat signal for Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s next industry-moving releases.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Kimi continues to challenge the frontier with K3.1 Pro

 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 Let AI sign in without sharing your passwords

 Canva’s first in-house image model climbs the ranks

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 MOONSHOT AI
 🌙  Kimi continues to challenge the frontier with K3.1 Pro
 Image source: Moonshot

 The Rundown: Chinese AI lab Moonshot just introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro, an upgrade to its July K3 model that it says is “matching the strongest proprietary models” on key benchmarks, with free-to-download weights set to come by Nov. 4.
 The details:
 Artificial Analysis placed it No. 4 overall on its Intelligence Index, beating OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and trailing only Anthropic’s 5.5 duo and Meta’s Muse Wonder.

 In Moonshot’s tests, K3.1 Pro tops Opus 5.5 on hours-long coding projects, expert academic questions, document-heavy research, and real-world job tasks.

 At $2 in/$10 out per million tokens, K3.1 Pro is priced like Sonnet 5.5, a fifth of Astra’s rate, but consumes tokens at a higher rate than its frontier rivals.

 AA also ranks it the best openly available cyber-defense model, scoring 64% with no safety refusals, trailing just a GPT-6 variant available only to vetted defenders.

 Why it matters: U.S. labs have kept their best hacking models locked down, but a Chinese model now sits just behind OAI’s gated cyber model. Dario Amodei gave defenders 6-12 months in May before Chinese models catch up, and K3.1 Pro is already near the top on defense — with open models’ attack skills also likely not far behind.

 TOGETHER WITH GARTNER
 💭  Rethink your enterprise app strategy        

 The Rundown: Megavendors still control enterprise software today, but for how long? With AI reshaping how apps are built and licensed, this Gartner webinar shows how to use SaaS renewals for flexibility, cut hidden API costs, and govern AI outcomes.
 In this webinar, you'll learn how to:
 Escape vendor lock-in at renewal

 Avoid hidden API costs

 Prepare to govern AI outcomes

 Register today .

 THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE
 💡   The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.
 Jonah, Head of AI Education: My wife and I used ChatGPT to bring our vision for a new master bedroom to life instead of hiring a designer.
 We started by sketching the basic layout, which ChatGPT rendered into a floor plan. We identified the wood, the type of cut we wanted, and the finishes. Then we had a detailed conversation about what we wanted the room to look like from each side.
 For smaller details, we scanned Google Images and Pinterest for inspiration pictures and designs we liked. We used ChatGPT Voice for back-and-forth conversations and final tweaks, re-rendering the images as our ideas developed.
 We took the final images to our contractor to help him understand the higher-level vision we wanted to achieve.
 Jennifer, Tech & Robotics Writer: We’re narrowing down high school options for my daughter, who wants to focus on art. I’m using Astra to find public schools in our area and beyond with strong art programs and understand how they compare.
 Astra can research school rankings and academic results, review art courses and facilities, and bring admissions requirements, portfolio expectations, fees, and commute times into one clear comparison. It can also suggest preparation classes—such as drawing, painting, digital art, or portfolio workshops—based on what each school expects.
 From there, it’s helping me build a shortlist, organize open days and application deadlines, and prepare questions for school visits. We can work through the options together and find a school she’s excited about.

 AI TRAINING
 🔐  Let AI sign in without sharing your passwords

 The Rundown: In this guide, you will use 1Password to approve an AI assistant’s login without pasting a password into chat. You’ll deny one request, test a small reading task, and check that access ends when you’re done.
 Step-by-step:
 Check whether your agent has the official 1Password connection. Muse and Grok Bot are rolling it out, while Claude has a separate Mac setup

 Choose a test account with no private data or saved payment details. Save its login in 1Password and sign out in the browser the agent will use

 Give the agent a page to read and rule out edits, messages, and purchases. Check the site and saved login in the 1Password request, then deny the request

 Start again and approve the correct test login. Check that the agent reads the right page without changing anything or asking for a password in chat

 Stop the task, sign out of the website, and remove the 1Password connection. Check the browser as well as the connection settings

 Pro tip: Removing a password connection may leave a website signed in. Check both before you finish.

 PRESENTED BY OPENART
 🎨   Create ad variations to scale performance marketing

 The Rundown: Have an ad that’s performing well? Or an ad format that inspires you? OpenArt’s Ad Remake makes it easy to create your own versions with your product, branding, and style — giving you more ads to test without starting from scratch.
 OpenArt Ad Remake lets you:
 Keep the hook, pacing, and structure that work

 Swap in your product, characters, and language without reshooting

 Adapt ads to 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, and 4:5 formats

 Try Ad Remake .

 CANVA
 🎨  Canva’s first in-house image model climbs the ranks
 Image source: Canva

 The Rundown: Canva just launched Craft, the company’s first in-house AI image model, debuting at No. 4 on DesignArena’s crowdsourced leaderboard behind only three OpenAI models.
 The details:
 Craft was trained on millions of designer-made templates like menus, slides, and posters from the company’s own library.

 The model plans each layout before drawing it with a two-step architecture, so images convert easily into editable designs via a Magic Layers feature.

 Craft’s 1340 score on the DesignArena beats the top models from Microsoft, Google, and xAI, while also landing No. 1 overall in portrait and nature categories.

 Craft is live for all Canva platform users and via public API, with MCP access for external assistants and agents also on the way.

 Why it matters: Canva has an endless supply of training data, and Craft’s strong results show how powerful that can be for building an in-house model. While legacy competitors have been reeling amid the AI boom, Canva’s integrations and now its own AI model put near frontier-level image capabilities in front of 250M+ users on its own terms.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Bridget built a gym log that updates itself every Friday
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Bridget Overson :
 “Every Friday at 10 a.m. ET, a scheduled Claude agent refreshes a living 'Hevy Workout Log' document with that week's strength-training data, body measurements, and a progress photo. The automation runs fully unattended, with no human in the loop after the owner sets it up.
 The agent pulls information from three independent systems: the Hevy fitness-tracking API, a Google Drive photo folder, and the living document. It reconciles those sources against a date range, determines what's new versus already recorded, and writes structured, formatted updates in the correct places. This requires more judgment than a simple script or webhook.
 Claude Docs, through a Claude Artifact, is the living document: it has one tab for each weekday and a Weekly Summary tab. There is no custom backend, database, or glue code. Because the workflow runs on a schedule without anyone watching, its specification requires a notification every time, including when nothing changed.”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

blogs.title: SAP's Philipp Herzig on AI built for business data
blogs.author: Melina Panitsidis
blogs.description: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}. AI coding tools can spin up an app in minutes, and plenty…
blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}. AI coding tools can spin up an app in minutes, and plenty of people have taken that as a sign traditional software is finished. SAP’s CTO thinks they’re missing the harder part: running a business on that app.
 In partnership with SAP , we sat down with CTO Philipp Herzig to talk about the “SaaS is dead” debate, how AI is changing the way people use work software, what agents need to know to get answers right, how to keep AI bills in check, and the models built for business data.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 What the “SaaS is dead” narrative misses

 From clicking screens to stating intent

 Teaching AI how your business runs

 Cheaper tokens, better business outcomes

 Specialized AI for decisions that count

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 INDUSTRY TAKE
 🏢  What the “SaaS is dead” narrative misses
 Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

 The Rundown: As AI coding tools let anyone build apps, many believe traditional software companies are over. Herzig thinks this narrative confuses building an app with running one, and says the same gap explains why so many AI pilots never make it to production.
 Cheung: What’s one AI trend you think is overhyped?
 Herzig: The idea that “SaaS is dead” because AI can now write software. It confuses the ability to generate an application with the responsibility of running it.
 Generating an expense app is one thing. Running it across 40 countries, keeping up with tax rules, enforcing permissions, and reconciling reimbursements is another. As agents take on more autonomous work, they depend more on trusted data, business context, governance, and security. The interface can change radically. The need for reliable business processes doesn’t.
 Cheung: Why do so many AI pilots never get deployed?
 Herzig: The difference between a prototype and a production-ready system at enterprise scale, with all the technological dependencies and complexity under the hood while still looking simple for the user, is still substantial human work.
 Cheung: What’s been harder at SAP, the technology or adoption?
 Herzig: Adoption, without a doubt. Useful AI changes who makes which decisions and how. That affects expertise, authority, and professional identity.
 The companies moving fastest gave access to people whose judgment the organization already trusted. A respected supply chain manager saying “this helped me catch a disruption” is more powerful than any training program.
 Why it matters: SAP has an obvious stake in defending enterprise software, but the gap between generating an app and running a business on it is real. If you’re rolling out AI at work, his adoption advice applies regardless of vendor: pick one high-value use case and put the colleagues people already trust first in line.

 AI IRL
 💻 From clicking screens to stating intent
 Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

 The Rundown: SAP’s newest AI push, Joule Work, flips how people use business software: instead of clicking through screens, you say what you want done. Herzig walked us through how it works, how he uses it himself, and what it means for developers.
 Cheung: How does Joule Work change the day-to-day experience of using business software?
 Herzig: For decades, enterprise software required us to learn its structure: which application to open, which screen to find, which buttons to click. With Joule Work , you start with what you want to accomplish. It brings together information and capabilities across applications.
 But this isn’t about replacing every screen with a chat box. With Spaces, Joule can turn your intent into a personalized visual workspace: a chart, table, or dashboard you refine by asking. I don’t have to log into four systems, orient myself, and hope I’m looking at the right data. The relevant picture is already assembled. Web, desktop, mobile, and voice let you work in the way that fits the moment.
 Cheung: What’s one way you use it yourself?
 Herzig: As CTO, I want to stay close to what our engineers are building. But the question for me isn’t just “What changed?” It’s “Where would my attention be useful?” Instead of piecing together an update, I can ask Joule to bring the relevant changes together. That helps me arrive at a team conversation better informed: what should we discuss, what needs a closer look, and where can I help?
 Joule doesn’t make those judgments for me. It reduces the work of gathering the information behind them. I spend less time collecting status and more time having conversations that move the work forward.
 Cheung: If anyone can build with AI, what’s left for developers to do?
 Herzig: The job shifts from implementation to architecture and judgment: deciding what’s worth building, evaluating business correctness, designing the system that governs agents safely, and handling edge cases and failures. The hardest engineering challenges in enterprise AI aren’t about building something that works. They’re about building something that works safely, at scale, with the right guardrails in place.
 Joule Studio (SAP’s tool for building custom AI agents) removes that baseline burden. Developers start with the enterprise context, such as authentication, permissions, and compliance, already in place and focus on what delivers value.
 Why it matters: If your company is handing employees agents and AI coding tools, Herzig’s point is that the easy part got easier and the hard part didn’t. Someone still has to own whether the output is correct, secure, and safe to act on, and that job is landing on developers.

 EDUCATING AI
 🧠   Teaching AI how your business runs
 Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Herzig says the riskiest AI answers are “fluent-but-wrong”: confident, correctly worded, and blind to how the business runs. SAP’s fix is giving agents a map of what company data means, plus a record of how past decisions got made.
 Cheung: Most people might think giving AI access to their company’s files is enough context. What does AI actually need to know about a business to get answers right?
 Herzig: Enterprise data lives in tables, and knowing what a field means requires understanding the business process behind it: the transactions, the unwritten rules and exceptions, and identity, like knowing a supplier in procurement is the same entity in finance.
 The main risk in enterprise AI is fluent-but-wrong: an answer that sounds authoritative but is contextually off.
 Cheung: SAP’s Knowledge Graph maps what a company’s data means. How does that make AI better in a business context?
 Herzig: It gives models a machine-readable map of business objects, relationships, and rules. Agents stop guessing what fields mean.
 That improves accuracy, reduces incorrect API calls and retries, and can give smaller models enough context for more tasks. But understanding a rule isn’t the same as enforcing it: actions still run with the user’s permissions, defined boundaries, and human approval where required.
 Cheung: SAP is also building Company Memory to capture how work actually gets done. What’s the most useful thing it stores?
 Herzig: The most valuable thing it stores is why an exception was approved: the context, rationale, authority, and outcome. The next person doesn’t have to start from scratch.
 An exception must not become a rule just because it worked once. A human process owner must review it to understand why the decision worked, whether the conditions still apply, and whether it is safe to generalize.
 Why it matters: If your team is wiring agents into real workflows, more documents in the prompt won’t fix fluent-but-wrong answers. An easy check: feed the agent inputs your real system would reject, like an invoice with no currency, and see what it accepts.

 TOKENOMICS
 💸   Cheaper tokens, better business outcomes
 Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Token prices keep falling, but company AI bills keep rising as usage spreads. Herzig says the question is shifting from who has the smartest model to who gets the best business result for the lowest cost.
 Cheung: What did SAP learn as employee AI use grew?
 Herzig: We cannot blindly throw everything at LLMs. An email summary doesn’t need the same model as complex, multi-step business reasoning. Route tasks by complexity, risk, and context, or solve them without an LLM call.
 Reduce unnecessary token consumption without losing relevant context, including running models locally where it makes sense, so that only what actually requires LLM reasoning reaches the model. Keep models replaceable as quality and costs improve. And test at production scale: more than 60,000 SAP colleagues use Joule Work internally.
 Cheung: Where do companies waste the most money on AI?
 Herzig: Sending everything to frontier models, and “context bloat”: excessive, low-value information. A cheap model that is unreliable at scale isn’t a good trade either. The goal is the best outcome at the lowest possible cost.
 Cheung: McKinsey found 80% of AI users feel more productive, but only 6% of companies see significant profit impact. What else closes that gap?
 Herzig: In knowledge-intensive industries, people are the primary cost, so faster research, drafting, and coding can translate into margin. In capital-intensive businesses, assets, energy, and logistics can matter far more than payroll. Here, better demand forecasts or maintenance decisions may have a larger impact than faster writing. That’s why we invest in tabular AI. It’s ideal for predicting values in structured business data.
 Why it matters: If your company’s AI costs are climbing, start with Herzig’s two culprits: top-tier models doing work a smaller one could handle, and prompts stuffed with information the model doesn’t need. And if your business runs on assets more than people, the bigger payoff may come from better forecasts, not faster writing.

 TABULAR AI
 📊   Specialized AI for decisions that count
 Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Tabular AI brings the foundation-model approach to spreadsheets and databases, and the space is heating up. SAP built its own SAP-RPT models, acquired Prior Labs, and committed more than €1B to it over four years, while Google and NVIDIA have also released tabular models of their own.
 Cheung: For a company that’s never used a tabular model, what’s a good first problem to try?
 Herzig: Start with use cases like payment delay prediction or cash flow forecasting. For payment delays, you need historical invoice dates, due dates, actual payment dates, customers, amounts, and a few contextual attributes.
 With a few thousand rows, a Tabular Foundation Model can begin predicting when a customer will pay and flag likely delays while you still have options. Reducing average collection time from 50 to 45 days at a large company can free up tens of millions in cash.
 Cheung: How can people judge whether to trust a prediction?
 Herzig: SAP-RPT-1.6 offers Explain by Feature, showing which variables influenced a prediction, and Explain by Example, showing similar historical records used as evidence. A finance controller can assess whether those patterns still apply.
 The longer-term ambition is causal reasoning: not just predicting a late payment, but understanding which intervention, such as a change of payment terms, would change it. That’s a research direction beyond explaining a prediction.
 Why it matters: If most of your company’s AI use is chat and writing help, this is a low-cost way to test something different. The late-payment data already sits in most finance systems, the payoff is easy to measure, and the explanations let your finance team check the model’s work.

 GO DEEPER
 🎟️ Join the SAP TechEd experience
 Herzig is scheduled to deliver the SAP TechEd keynote on Oct. 27, kicking off three days of virtual sessions on building AI-powered systems that move from intent to execution.
 Register for the virtual event ....

blogs.title: Anthropic S-1 Analysis: How 7 Key Metrics Stack Up
blogs.description: Anthropic filed their S-11 this week, the largest AI listing yet. Founded in 2021 by Dario & Daniela Amodei, the company has grown from a…
blogs.content:
Anthropic filed their S-1 1 this week, the largest AI listing yet.

 Founded in 2021 by Dario & Daniela Amodei, the company has grown from a research lab into the second-largest model developer, selling Claude to more than 11,900 customers who spend over $100,000 a year. The comparisons below set the reported OpenAI figures 2 against Anthropic’s derived gross margin 3 , adjusted operating margin 4 & compute commitments 5 .

 Anthropic generated $16.3B of revenue in the first six months of 2026, a fourteen-fold increase over the $1.2B of the first half of 2025. That half-year alone was more than three times all of 2025, when Anthropic grew 11.9-fold to $4.6B, more than four times OpenAI’s 253%.

 The second quarter was $11.6B against $4.7B in the first; revenue has nearly tripled for two consecutive quarters.

 Three straight years of roughly ten-fold growth: 9.4x, then 11.9x, then 14.0x.

 For example, with the release of Claude Fable 5.1 in September 2026, we reduced the cost of typical workloads by approximately 25% compared to Fable 5, with savings of up to 45% for complex coding & highly agentic tasks. Similarly, with the release of Opus 5.5 that same month, we reduced customers’ cost per task by approximately 40% compared to Opus 5.

 When Opus 4.5 launched in November 2025 with more capability & a lower cost per task than Opus 4.1, revenue growth accelerated from 48% quarter over quarter to 132% the following quarter. Jevon’s paradox in the real world.

 Anthropic is cash-flow positive. Operating loss was $8.1B in 2025 including a $1.5B copyright settlement. It narrowed every quarter of 2026, & in the second quarter Anthropic reported $974M of operating income, an 8.4% GAAP margin & 19% adjusted.

 Anthropic has distributed its computing needs evenly over four major providers. Broadcom, SpaceXAI, Google & AWS each hold between $110B & $161B of commitments, together four fifths of the $637B total.

 Anthropic carries essentially no drawn debt : the $15B revolver is undrawn & the only outstanding notes are $6.2B of non-interest-bearing Amazon convertibles. The leverage is instead in commitments. The filing discloses $265.6B of fixed or minimum guarantees at June 30, 2026 & a further $245B executed since.

 These businesses are forming a keiretsu : each entangled in the other’s equity, debt & go-to-market.

 Concentration has fallen : no single customer exceeded 10% of revenue for the nine months to September 30, 2026, & the top five were about 25%. That is different from 2025, when customers spending over $100,000 accounted for 76% of revenue.

 This pattern of initial deployment, demonstrated value, & rapid expansion has been replicated across organizations & is reflected in our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026.

 What is Anthropic worth? The case for a very large number is simple : a business that grew 11.9-fold on a 40% derived gross margin & has just begun earning an operating profit. The case against is equally simple : $637B of compute commitments, two thirds non-cancelable, against $4.6B of 2025 revenue, where revenue is consumption-based with no lock-in & the payments arrive whether customers do.

 Nearly half of Anthropic revenue is now delivered through market places, a natural progression of many enterprise companies.

 Anthropic’s S-1 describes an AI company with an enviable business model, explosive growth, & increasing efficiency.

 Congratulations to the Anthropic team on reaching this milestone. Building a business that went from $41M to a $16B half-year in three years is without precedent.

---

 Anthropic, PBC Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0002130357, accession 000162828026067168, filed October 26, 2026: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026067168/anthropicpbc-sx1.htm   ↩︎

 OpenAI figures are press-reported & unverified. Anthropic figures are from the S-1 filed October 26, 2026 (SEC EDGAR CIK 0002130357).  ↩︎

 Anthropic does not report gross margin. It changed in FY2025 from a functional presentation to one by nature of expense. The 40% is derived from Note 8, which retains cost of revenue: (4,585 - 2,773) / 4,585. The equivalent for the first half of 2026 is 85%: (16,286 - 2,380) / 16,286. Both are my calculations, not disclosed figures.  ↩︎

 Adjusted operating income excludes stock-based compensation, non-cash charitable contributions & the Bartz settlement. FY2025 adjusted operating loss was $4.9B against a GAAP $8.1B.  ↩︎

 The $637B of commitments is the sum of seven named agreements in the filing: Broadcom $161.2B, SpaceXAI up to $120.5B, Google at least $114.5B, Amazon at least $110.0B, Microsoft at least $44.9B, Nscale up to $44.6B & Lambda approximately $41.3B. The filing does not disclose an aggregate total; that figure is my arithmetic. Google, Amazon, Microsoft & Broadcom are “at least” commitments that are non-cancelable with true-up clauses. SpaceXAI may be cancelled by either party on 90 days’ notice after initial periods ending January & March 2027. Nscale & Lambda accrue fees only as capacity is delivered.  ↩︎

blogs.title: The End of the Internet
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it's just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears.
blogs.content:
The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it's just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress.

It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install!

I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable , an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever.

The End of Blogs

2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet ; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom , also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space:

Talking Points Memo , Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000

Instapundit , Little Green Footballs , and Dooce launched in 2001

Matt Yglesias , Daily Kos , Eschaton , The Volokh Conspiracy , Power Line , Gizmodo , Gawker , paidContent , and Daring Fireball launched in 2002

Ezra Klein , Marginal Revolution , ReadWriteWeb , and AVC launched in 2003

That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference.

Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain.

Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business.

For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future :

It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost…

I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone.

In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for.

The End of Social Media

Google wasn’t the only Aggregator: a decade later there was a new means of discovery, which was social media. Now instead of searching for a site you could have a link shared directly to you, not just by email but on a site that served up interesting updates about whomever you chose to follow. And, for a period of time, followers could become friends. Stratechery’s fortunate timing was not just in terms of subscriptions becoming technically viable, but also the fact that Twitter was a community, not unlike the early Internet: genuinely interesting conversations happened in public, and you could reply-guy your way to broader distribution.

Social media was also free, however, and even easier to get started than a blog ever was; that meant that the amount of content was greater by many orders of magnitude. This meant that algorithms started to matter — Facebook had one relatively early, but it took Twitter much longer — and also anyone with any sort of prominence had to start taking a much more defensive approach. Community, sadly, doesn’t scale; any platform that is available to everyone starts out special and spirals from there. Ultimately, public social media sites became personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement, culminating in TikTok, a social media site with basically zero social component.

However, that doesn’t mean social networking went away: in fact, I think that social networking is stronger than ever; the difference is that it isn’t public, but is rather in group chats. Group chats are familiar, they are high trust, they are, in many respects, the best of the Internet: even as technology atomizes us the group chat is the only place you can connect with people you care about, anytime and anywhere.

In other words, the redemption of social media was — just like blogging — to become smaller. The scaling that mattered for most people was not an ever larger audience, but a proliferation of infinite finite groups. Social media 1.0 , even at its best, followed the 90-9-1 rule: one percent spoke, nine percent commented, and 90 percent lurked; the magic of group chats is not in giving everyone a voice, but a place where you feel safe to talk.

The End of the Internet

The PHP vulnerabilities were just two of a host of security issues last week alone; there were also:

Compromised intermediate CA private keys (although this was an example of sheer incompetence, not AI hacking)

Major new vulnerabilities in Node.js, GitLab, Java, and Cisco products

Breaches in LiteLLM’s supply chain and Railway developer platform

This is, believe it or not, only a partial list, and I expect things to only get worse. All of software is built on an inherently creaky human-authored foundation; the human factor meant the primary gate in all of software development was “Did it work?”, not “Is it secure from every possible privilege escalation or race condition?” or the myriad of ways that software can act in ways not intended.

The saving factor previously is that attackers were limited by human time and ingenuity as well; AI, however, has limitless time and the ability to substitute iteration for cleverness — and it’s getting pretty clever as well! It’s not a surprise that this wave of vulnerabilities is coming to light, and it’s going to get worse before it gets better — which I do, for the record, expect to happen; after all, the good guys have AI as well, and in the long run software will be better when it is (re)written by AI, and defended by agents continuously.

At the same time, what this entails is that the public Internet, to an even greater extent than now, will be a battle zone at best (i.e. social media), and a wasteland at worst (everything else). Some of this is economic, as AI consumes everything — both content and attention — without giving any of the traffic back that Google did, but it is also technical: it was already a dodgy proposition to stand up your own site or app, which was the very promise of the Internet, given the hacking risks; in the age of AI it’s madness.

It is sad. When I was a kid we called up BBS’s that were hosted in people’s homes; when I was in high school we downloaded music from public FTP addresses; when I was in college we set up our own websites. Anyone could set up a server, and that server was just as much a part of the Internet as any other server; that’s simply not viable any longer, even if you weren’t worried about making money. The Internet as we knew it is dead.

There are, however, green shoots of possibility, and once again the answer is to go smaller. When anyone can make an app, the answer is not to try and make a quick buck in the App Store; in fact, the surge in slop will make the market worse for everyone. Rather, it’s to make something for yourself and a small group of trusted friends and colleagues.

This is exactly what has happened at Stratechery: we have made a bunch of different apps, for everything from podcast production to task trackers to calendar management, none of which will ever be made available publicly. That doesn’t even include the apps made for oneself: I’ve created a bunch of different apps to manage my house and sports viewing: it turns out I had a lot of software-shaped holes in my life that suddenly I can fill without asking permission.

Software has always been different from physical goods in that its zero marginal cost nature meant it could scale to far more people; at the same time, the sheer amount of up-front effort involved in creating it meant that the intended audience needed to be large enough to justify the investment. AI completely changes that: suddenly it’s possible to create software for one person, or one team; smaller target audiences aren’t just a necessity for security, they’re an entirely new and potentially much larger market for software creation at scale, by literally everyone. Or, to use the example above, the group chat era of software is here and it’s going to be so much better than what came before.
